Read terms ABSTRACT: Maternal hemorrhage, defined as a cumulative blood loss of greater than or equal to 1,000 mL or blood loss accompanied by signs or symptoms of hypovolemia within 24 hours after the birth process, remains the leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide 1. Additional important secondary sequelae from hemorrhage exist and include adult respiratory distress syndrome, shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute renal failure, loss of fertility, and pituitary necrosis (Sheehan syndrome). Hemorrhage that leads to blood transfusion is the leading cause of severe maternal morbidity in the United States closely followed by disseminated intravascular coagulation 2. In the United States, the rate of postpartum hemorrhage increased 26% between 1994 and 2006 primarily because of increased rates of atony 3. In contrast, maternal mortality from postpartum obstetric hemorrhage has decreased since the late 1980s and accounted for slightly more than 10% of maternal mortalities (approximately 1.7 deaths per 100,000 live births) in 2009 2 4. This observed decrease in mortality is associated with increasing rates of transfusion and peripartum hysterectomy 2 3 4. The purpose of this Practice Bulletin is to discuss the risk factors for postpartum hemorrhage as well as its evaluation, prevention, and management. In addition, this document will encourage obstetrician–gynecologists and other obstetric care providers to play key roles in implementing standardized bundles of care (eg, policies, guidelines, and algorithms) for the management of postpartum hemorrhage. fetched_contents.text: Q&A: Boosting consistency when reporting postpartum hemorrhage Q: What are the most common reasons postpartum hemorrhage is documented and coded inconsistently, and how can coders and clinicians help address these issues? A: As one of the top five causes of maternal mortality worldwide, postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is a global challenge that impacts maternity units everywhere and must be taken seriously by healthcare systems. Preventing PPH requires timely recognition, availability of appropriate resources, and appropriate responses. According to hemorrhage-associated maternal mortality ratios published by the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology, there is a higher ratio of PPH for non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic patients compared to non-Hispanic white patients, highlighting why equity and standardization are critical in addressing PPH. Many drivers for coding PPH tend to be related to processes and documentation rather than clinical causes. Specific non-clinical causes include documentation of estimated blood loss, template errors, lack of standardized definitions, and absence of coding and CDI reviews. Inconsistent documentation can make it hard to identify true hemorrhage cases, and electronic templates may not always be aligned with current clinical practices, leading to codes that do not represent the true clinical picture of patients. There should be a specific place to document estimated blood loss with consistent measurement guidelines available across all template types. Additionally, different teams should not be using different criteria for what qualifies as a PPH. Without an extra layer of review from audits, important details can miss these differences, impacting both data integrity and care insights. Standardized criteria should also be available to distinguish PPH from what is considered normal postoperative or normal postpartum bleeding. A lack of clarity will impact coding, reporting, and even accurate benchmarking, particularly when one provider's hemorrhage is another person's normal. Before outcomes can be improved, measurements have to be agreed upon. As for the coding side, coding pathways may default to PPH whenever uterine atony with a mention of bleeding is documented, even if the clinical picture does not meet the criteria. If there is no formal audit process for PPH coding accuracy, these cases could end up completely excluded from reviews, creating a blind spot in review processes. Improving outcomes goes beyond clinical interventions and into fixing the systems that support care delivery. To resolve these non-clinical issues, coding and CDI teams should start with standardizing definitions, redesigning templates, improving documentation workflows, and expanding reviews into targeted cases. Because accurate documentation of estimated blood loss is the cornerstone of identifying PPH early, teams should work with nursing and together implement focused initiatives that are all about measurement consistency. For example, set a standard for using weight based on milliliter measurements. Then focus on programming electronic record systems to automatically convert measurements to milliliters so that no mental calculations are required to maintain consistency. Adopting the definition of PPH by the American College of Obstetrics and Gynecologists can also keep teams on the same page. With everyone playing by the same rules, clinical templates should be revised to include mandatory sections for estimated blood loss through documentation prompts so that providers can’t skip this critical step. Finally, adding peer-to-peer education on coding and CDI queries will further encourage consistency across teams. Now focusing in on the coding and CDI world further, determine if coding trees are actually leading coders straight to PPH whenever uterine atony or bleeding are mentioned, because even the best documentation can't guarantee accurate data if coding pathways are flawed. According to Coding Clinic, routine or expected hemorrhage during delivery is not supposed to be reported unless the provider documents that the bleeding is excessive or is a complication. If the documentation is unclear, coders should query the provider, not just report a code from ICD-10-CM category O72, Postpartum hemorrhage. Building query templates for both coding and CDI teams further ensures consistency, which can help close the gap between the clinical reality at the bedside and the coded data. Editor’s note: This question and answer were excerpted from the HCPro webinar, “Every Birth, Every Mother: Partnering to Reduce Postpartum Hemorrhage with Excellence,” presented by Laura Ogaard, RN, MSN, CCDS, director of education for Intermountain Physician Services, and Sathya Vijayakumar, MS, MBA, LSSGB, director with Intermountain Physician Advisor Services, Clinical Excellence. It originally appeared in JustCoding.

Published in final edited form as: Am J Obstet Gynecol MFM. 2022 Sep 2;5(2 Suppl):100740. doi: 10.1016/j.ajogmf.2022.100740 Abstract Postpartum hemorrhage remains a leading cause of maternal morbidity and mortality in the United States. Several state maternal morbidity and mortality committees have reviewed areas of opportunity concerning postpartum hemorrhage management and found that common patterns include delays in recognition and response to hemorrhage. Hospital systems and state perinatal quality collaboratives have found that comprehensive, interdisciplinary response to postpartum hemorrhage care improves patient outcomes and, in some instances, reduces racial disparities. A key component of this focus involves the implementation of stage-based hemorrhage protocols for postpartum hemorrhage management. Stage-based hemorrhage protocols are designed to reduce delays in the diagnosis and management and avoid the pitfalls of cognitive biases. These protocols are complex, and their effectiveness is tied to the quality of their implementation. Systematic benchmarking and development of quality metrics for adherence to postpartum hemorrhage bundles would be expected to improve clinical outcomes, but evidence regarding the effectiveness of this practice in the literature is limited. Here, key features of stage-based interventions and evidence regarding the use of quality metrics for postpartum hemorrhage protocol adherence have been outlined. Keywords: maternal death, obstetrical labor complications, postpartum hemorrhage, pregnancy, quality improvement Evidence for postpartum hemorrhage management protocols as systems issues Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) management involves a team of clinicians working in a coordinated fashion to obtain hemostasis and manage the effects of acute blood loss. Thus, when opportunities in outcomes after PPH are found, they are often related to systems-level factors.1,2 For example, a PPH event might raise any of the following potential quality issues: 1. Access: Has the patient had the opportunity to seek timely prenatal care to have risk factors optimized (eg, identification and treatment of peripartum anemia)? Did they deliver in a nonhospital setting (eg, home) because of the lack of access to hospital care, resulting in delayed management? 2. Structure: Does the hospital have the equipment in place to address hemorrhage, such as the provision of standardized hemorrhage carts and ready access to uterotonics? Are hospital teams prepared to respond to PPH via participation in team training and simulations for PPH management? Does the hospital have a standardized stage-based management protocol that teams have been trained to follow? 3. Process: How is blood loss measured and communicated to team members during acute hemorrhage? Several state maternal morbidity and mortality committees have reviewed areas of opportunity concerning PPH management and found that common patterns include delays in recognition and response to hemorrhage.1,2 These findings were consistent with previous work demonstrating that preventable maternal mortality is often a function of delays in seeking care, arriving at a health facility, and provision of adequate care.4 Delays in postpartum hemorrhage recognition and postpartum hemorrhage response Providers find it difficult to precisely estimate blood loss. Obstetrical literature indicates certain patterns exist, including overestimation in low-volume blood loss events, and underestimation in higher blood loss deliveries (ie, provider estimates are biased toward the median blood loss). Underestimation of blood loss during PPH can result in delays in the diagnosis and management, which have been associated with maternal mortalities.1 Quantitative blood loss (QBL) has been proposed as an alternative approach intended to reduce these cognitive biases. QBL can be performed using traditional gravimetric and volumetric techniques, such as graduated under buttock drapes, and weighing of laparotomy pads and irrigation canisters; it can also be performed using newer techniques, such as adding real-time imaging of laparotomy pads and irrigation canisters.5 These techniques have been shown to be more accurate than estimated blood loss compared with “gold standard methodologies,” such as hemoglobin change, but disappointingly have not yet been shown to alter clinical outcomes.6 There are several potential pitfalls for QBL in practice, which may limit its effectiveness. Practitioners can focus on the attainment of an “accurate” QBL value at the expense of a timely QBL value, resulting in time delays in the recognition of hemorrhage. QBL that does not facilitate early recognition of the onset or severity of hemorrhage is not useful. Recommended documentation elements and structure for obstetric records

ACOG and related guidance emphasize that documentation in obstetric records serves management of care, communication, quality assurance, and record keeping, and that standardized forms and checklists can improve standardization and communication [N2-R2][N2-R3]. For postpartum hemorrhage specifically, documentation should be structured around the hemorrhage event itself, the interventions provided, and the subsequent follow-up and disposition, with special attention to blood loss and its measurement.

## What should be recorded about the hemorrhage event?
The hemorrhage event should be documented with enough detail to support clinical decision-making and later review. ACOG guidance notes that maternal hemorrhage is defined as cumulative blood loss of ≥1,000 mL or blood loss accompanied by signs or symptoms of hypovolemia within 24 hours after birth [N1-F1]. Although the evidence here does not give a single ACOG-specific “template” for every event, the broader obstetric record guidance supports including standardized, structured documentation [N2-R1]. For hemorrhage documentation, the key elements are:

- Time of onset and duration of bleeding.
- Estimated blood loss (EBL) or quantitative blood loss (QBL), including the method used and any discrepancy between provider estimate and measured value [N4-F4][N5-F3].
- Clinical signs and symptoms, such as hypotension, tachycardia, pallor, or altered mental status, that indicate hypovolemia [N1-F1].
- Any precipitating factors or risk factors present, such as uterine atony, retained placenta, or trauma [N1-F1][N6-R3].
- Whether the hemorrhage was recognized promptly and whether it was considered excessive or a complication [N4-F4].

The evidence base here also points to the importance of standardized definitions and consistent measurement guidelines, because inconsistent documentation can make it hard to identify true hemorrhage cases and can affect coding, reporting, and benchmarking [N4-F4]. Therefore, the documentation should include a clear statement that the bleeding was not normal postpartum bleeding and that it was clinically significant enough to require intervention [N4-F4].

## How to document interventions and dosages
Interventions and dosages should be documented in a way that supports defensibility and continuity of care. ACOG guidance stresses the need for standardized bundles of care, including policies, guidelines, and algorithms, and notes that prompt escalation to other interventions such as tamponade or surgical techniques is recommended when uterotonics fail [N1-F1][N6-R3]. The documentation should therefore include:

- The sequence of interventions used, such as administration of uterotonics, manual removal of retained placenta, or uterine massage.
- Dosages and routes of administration for all drugs, including uterotonic agents and any transfusions [N4-F4].
- Whether intravenous fluids, blood products, or other supportive measures were used.
- Whether surgical interventions were performed and, if so, the type and indication [N6-R3].

The evidence from the ACDIS Q&A is especially useful here because it explicitly states that accurate documentation of estimated blood loss is the cornerstone of identifying PPH early, and that electronic templates should be revised to include mandatory sections for estimated blood loss and to program systems to convert measurements automatically [N4-F4]. It also recommends using weight-based milliliter measurements and avoiding mental calculations so that documentation is consistent across providers [N4-F4]. This suggests that the documentation should not only record what was done, but also how it was measured and why it was needed.

## How to document follow-up and disposition
Follow-up and disposition should be clearly documented to show the course of the hemorrhage and the patient’s response to treatment. ACOG guidance emphasizes evaluation, prevention, and management, and states that standardized bundles of care are recommended [N1-F1]. The documentation should therefore include:

- The patient’s hemodynamic status after intervention, including blood pressure, heart rate, and urine output.
- Any transfusion requirements and the volume administered.
- Whether the patient was admitted for further observation or transferred to a higher-level facility.
- The final diagnosis or disposition, such as “postpartum hemorrhage managed medically,” “hemorrhage with uterine atony,” or “hemorrhage requiring surgical intervention” [N4-F4].

The evidence also supports including alerts and documentation prompts in the electronic health record (EHR) to ensure that follow-up information is captured systematically [N4-R4][N6-R4]. In addition, the ACDIS guidance stresses that different teams should not use different criteria for what qualifies as PPH and that standardized criteria should be available to distinguish PPH from normal postoperative or normal postpartum bleeding [N4-F4]. Therefore, the follow-up documentation should explicitly state whether the event met the PPH criteria and whether it was considered a complication.

## Practical documentation structure
Putting these elements together, a recommended documentation structure for postpartum hemorrhage would include:

1. **Event description**: Time, duration, bleeding characteristics, and whether it was recognized as abnormal.
2. **Blood loss measurement**: Estimated or quantitative blood loss, method used, and any discrepancy [N4-F4][N5-F3].
3. **Clinical features**: Signs and symptoms of hypovolemia, risk factors, and precipitating factors [N1-F1].
4. **Interventions and dosages**: Sequence, type, route, and dose of interventions [N6-R3][N4-F4].
5. **Follow-up and disposition**: Hemodynamic status, transfusion, admission, transfer, and final diagnosis [N4-F4].
6. **Alerts and prompts**: Mandatory sections for estimated blood loss and standardized prompts to improve consistency [N4-F4].

Overall, the evidence supports a structured, standardized, and consistent approach to documenting postpartum hemorrhage, with emphasis on measurable blood loss, intervention sequence, and clear follow-up [N2-R2][N2-R3][N4-F4].

Recommended documentation elements and structure for obstetric records

ACOG and related guidance emphasize that documentation in obstetric records serves management of care, communication, quality assurance, and record keeping, and that standardized forms and checklists can improve standardization and communication [N2-R2][N2-R3]. For postpartum hemorrhage specifically, documentation should be structured around the hemorrhage event itself, the interventions provided, and the subsequent follow-up and disposition, with special attention to blood loss and its measurement.

## What should be recorded about the hemorrhage event?
The hemorrhage event should be documented with enough detail to support clinical decision-making and later review. ACOG guidance notes that maternal hemorrhage is defined as cumulative blood loss of ≥1,000 mL or blood loss accompanied by signs or symptoms of hypovolemia within 24 hours after birth [N1-F1]. Although the evidence here does not give a single ACOG-specific “template” for every event, the broader obstetric record guidance supports including standardized, structured documentation [N2-R1]. For hemorrhage documentation, the key elements are:

- Time of onset and duration of bleeding.
- Estimated blood loss (EBL) or quantitative blood loss (QBL), including the method used and any discrepancy between provider estimate and measured value [N4-F4][N5-F3].
- Clinical signs and symptoms, such as hypotension, tachycardia, pallor, or altered mental status, that indicate hypovolemia [N1-F1].
- Any precipitating factors or risk factors present, such as uterine atony, retained placenta, or trauma [N1-F1][N6-R3].
- Whether the hemorrhage was recognized promptly and whether it was considered excessive or a complication [N4-F4].

The evidence base here also points to the importance of standardized definitions and consistent measurement guidelines, because inconsistent documentation can make it hard to identify true hemorrhage cases and can affect coding, reporting, and benchmarking [N4-F4]. Therefore, the documentation should include a clear statement that the bleeding was not normal postpartum bleeding and that it was clinically significant enough to require intervention [N4-F4].

## How to document interventions and dosages
Interventions and dosages should be documented in a way that supports defensibility and continuity of care. ACOG guidance stresses the need for standardized bundles of care, including policies, guidelines, and algorithms, and notes that prompt escalation to other interventions such as tamponade or surgical techniques is recommended when uterotonics fail [N1-F1][N6-R3]. The documentation should therefore include:

- The sequence of interventions used, such as administration of uterotonics, manual removal of retained placenta, or uterine massage.
- Dosages and routes of administration for all drugs, including uterotonic agents and any transfusions [N4-F4].
- Whether intravenous fluids, blood products, or other supportive measures were used.
- Whether surgical interventions were performed and, if so, the type and indication [N6-R3].

The evidence from the ACDIS Q&A is especially useful here because it explicitly states that accurate documentation of estimated blood loss is the cornerstone of identifying PPH early, and that electronic templates should be revised to include mandatory sections for estimated blood loss and to program systems to convert measurements automatically [N4-F4]. It also recommends using weight-based milliliter measurements and avoiding mental calculations so that documentation is consistent across providers [N4-F4]. This suggests that the documentation should not only record what was done, but also how it was measured and why it was needed.

## How to document follow-up and disposition
Follow-up and disposition should be clearly documented to show the course of the hemorrhage and the patient’s response to treatment. ACOG guidance emphasizes evaluation, prevention, and management, and states that standardized bundles of care are recommended [N1-F1]. The documentation should therefore include:

- The patient’s hemodynamic status after intervention, including blood pressure, heart rate, and urine output.
- Any transfusion requirements and the volume administered.
- Whether the patient was admitted for further observation or transferred to a higher-level facility.
- The final diagnosis or disposition, such as “postpartum hemorrhage managed medically,” “hemorrhage with uterine atony,” or “hemorrhage requiring surgical intervention” [N4-F4].

The evidence also supports including alerts and documentation prompts in the electronic health record (EHR) to ensure that follow-up information is captured systematically [N4-R4][N6-R4]. In addition, the ACDIS guidance stresses that different teams should not use different criteria for what qualifies as PPH and that standardized criteria should be available to distinguish PPH from normal postoperative or normal postpartum bleeding [N4-F4]. Therefore, the follow-up documentation should explicitly state whether the event met the PPH criteria and whether it was considered a complication.

## Practical documentation structure
Putting these elements together, a recommended documentation structure for postpartum hemorrhage would include:

1. **Event description**: Time, duration, bleeding characteristics, and whether it was recognized as abnormal.
2. **Blood loss measurement**: Estimated or quantitative blood loss, method used, and any discrepancy [N4-F4][N5-F3].
3. **Clinical features**: Signs and symptoms of hypovolemia, risk factors, and precipitating factors [N1-F1].
4. **Interventions and dosages**: Sequence, type, route, and dose of interventions [N6-R3][N4-F4].
5. **Follow-up and disposition**: Hemodynamic status, transfusion, admission, transfer, and final diagnosis [N4-F4].
6. **Alerts and prompts**: Mandatory sections for estimated blood loss and standardized prompts to improve consistency [N4-F4].

Overall, the evidence supports a structured, standardized, and consistent approach to documenting postpartum hemorrhage, with emphasis on measurable blood loss, intervention sequence, and clear follow-up [N2-R2][N2-R3][N4-F4].

It also states that accurate documentation of estimated blood loss is the cornerstone of identifying PPH early [N4-F4]. This means that documentation should not be delayed until after the event is resolved; rather, it should be captured promptly during the acute phase so that the clinical picture is preserved.

## When documentation should be completed during the event and after
During the event, documentation should be immediate and structured. The hemorrhage should be documented as soon as it is recognized, with key elements such as the time of onset, estimated or quantitative blood loss, signs of hypovolemia, and the interventions initiated [N4-F4][N5-F3]. The evidence also supports using electronic prompts and alerts to ensure that critical information is captured while the patient is still under acute management [N4-R4][N6-R4].

After the event, documentation should be completed promptly to preserve defensibility. ACDIS emphasizes that coding pathways may default to PPH whenever uterine atony with a mention of bleeding is documented, even if the clinical picture does not meet the criteria [N4-F4]. Therefore, documentation after the event should be thorough enough to support the clinical judgment that the hemorrhage was excessive or a complication rather than routine postpartum bleeding. This includes documenting the provider’s assessment that the bleeding was not normal, the estimated blood loss, and the interventions taken [N4-F4].

## Coding and billing implications
Coding and billing implications are heavily tied to documentation consistency. ACDIS states that coding pathways may lead to PPH being reported whenever uterine atony with bleeding is mentioned, even if the clinical picture does not meet the criteria [N4-F4]. It also notes that coding and CDI reviews should start with standardizing definitions, redesigning templates, improving documentation workflows, and expanding reviews into targeted cases [N4-F4]. This means that the documentation must be precise and aligned with the ACOG definition of maternal hemorrhage as ≥1,000 mL or blood loss accompanied by signs or symptoms of hypovolemia within 24 hours after birth [N1-F1].

The coding guidance also specifies that routine or expected hemorrhage during delivery should not be reported unless the provider documents that the bleeding is excessive or is a complication [N4-F4]. This implies that the documentation must clearly state whether the hemorrhage was abnormal and whether it met the criteria for PPH. If the documentation is unclear, coders should query the provider rather than report a code from ICD-10-CM category O72, Postpartum hemorrhage [N4-F4].

## How to preserve defensibility and continuity of care
To preserve defensibility, documentation should be standardized, consistent, and defensible. ACDIS recommends standardizing definitions, redesigning templates, improving documentation workflows, and expanding reviews into targeted cases [N4-F4]. It also recommends that electronic templates be revised to include mandatory sections for estimated blood loss and that systems be programmed to convert measurements automatically to maintain consistency [N4-F4]. This supports the use of structured templates and prompts rather than relying on memory or inconsistent free text.

Continuity of care is preserved by documenting the hemorrhage in a way that can be understood by subsequent providers. The evidence emphasizes that documentation fulfills key functions including communication and quality assurance [N2-R3]. It also supports using standardized hemorrhage carts, ready access to uterotonics, and standardized stage-based management protocols to improve care [N5-F3]. Therefore, the documentation should include enough detail to allow others to understand the clinical course and the rationale for interventions.

## Practical workflow recommendations
A practical workflow would include:
1. Documenting the hemorrhage immediately upon recognition.
2. Recording estimated or quantitative blood loss and the method used.
3. Documenting clinical signs of hypovolemia and any precipitating factors [N1-F1].
4. Documenting interventions, dosages, and transfusions.
5. Documenting follow-up and disposition after the event.
6. Using prompts and alerts in the EHR to ensure completeness [N4-R4][N6-R4].
7. Including a clear statement that the bleeding was not normal and that it was clinically significant [N4-F4].

Overall, the evidence supports a workflow in which documentation is prompt, structured, consistent, and tied to the ACOG and ACDIS guidance on PPH criteria and coding [N1-F1][N4-F4]. This approach strengthens defensibility and supports continuity of care across the care team.

## What the obstetrician should know

As an obstetrician, the recommended structure for postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) documentation should be evidence-based, standardized, and defensible. The evidence here points to a clear framework that combines ACOG guidance on diagnosis and management with practical documentation, workflow, coding, and template considerations [N1-F1][N1-R1][N4-F4][N5-F3][N6-R4]. The core idea is that PPH documentation should support clinical decision-making, communication, quality assurance, and billing, while also preserving continuity of care and defensibility [N2-R3][N2-R2].

## 1) ACOG-specific diagnosis and management guidance

ACOG defines maternal hemorrhage as a cumulative blood loss of ≥1,000 mL or blood loss accompanied by signs or symptoms of hypovolemia within 24 hours after birth [N1-F1]. This is the threshold that should guide your clinical judgment and documentation. ACOG’s guidance also emphasizes risk factors, evaluation, prevention, and management, and recommends standardized bundles of care, including policies, guidelines, and algorithms [N1-F1]. It also supports formal assessment for hemorrhage risk at multiple points in prenatal, delivery, and postpartum care [N6-R4].

ACOG further recommends escalation when uterotonics fail to adequately control postpartum hemorrhage [N6-R3]. The evidence also supports stage-based hemorrhage protocols, which are designed to reduce delays in diagnosis and management and avoid cognitive biases [N5-F3]. This means that documentation should be tied to a structured protocol rather than an ad hoc response.

## 2) What should be recorded about the hemorrhage event?

The hemorrhage event should be documented with enough detail to support clinical decision-making and later review. Based on ACOG and related guidance, the documentation should include:

- **Time of onset and duration of bleeding**.
- **Estimated blood loss (EBL) or quantitative blood loss (QBL)**, including the method used and any discrepancy between provider estimate and measured value [N4-F4][N5-F3].
- **Clinical signs and symptoms of hypovolemia**, such as hypotension, tachycardia, pallor, or altered mental status [N1-F1].
- **Precipitating factors or risk factors**, such as uterine atony, retained placenta, or trauma [N1-F1][N6-R3].
- A clear statement that the bleeding was **not normal postpartum bleeding** and that it was clinically significant enough to require intervention [N4-F4].

ACOG guidance also supports standardized bundles of care and alerts, which help improve recognition and escalation [N1-F1][N6-R4]. The evidence from ACDIS adds that many coding drivers are tied to documentation rather than clinical causes, and that accurate documentation of estimated blood loss is the cornerstone of identifying PPH early [N4-F4].

## 3) How to document interventions and dosages

Interventions and dosages should be documented in a way that supports defensibility and continuity of care. ACOG emphasizes standardized bundles of care, including policies, guidelines, and algorithms, and notes that prompt escalation to other interventions such as tamponade or surgical techniques is recommended when uterotonics fail [N1-F1][N6-R3]. The documentation should therefore include:

- **Sequence of interventions** used, such as administration of uterotonics, manual removal of retained placenta, or uterine massage.
- **Dosages and routes of administration** for all drugs, including uterotonic agents and any transfusions [N4-F4].
- Whether **intravenous fluids, blood products, or other supportive measures** were used.
- Whether **surgical interventions** were performed and, if so, the type and indication [N6-R3].

The evidence also supports using electronic prompts and alerts in the EHR to ensure that critical information is captured while the patient is still under acute management [N4-R4][N6-R4]. ACDIS explicitly recommends that electronic templates be revised to include mandatory sections for estimated blood loss and that systems be programmed to convert measurements automatically to maintain consistency [N4-F4].

## 4) How to document follow-up and disposition

Follow-up and disposition should be clearly documented to show the course of the hemorrhage and the patient’s response to treatment. ACOG emphasizes evaluation, prevention, and management, and states that standardized bundles of care are recommended [N1-F1]. The documentation should therefore include:

- The patient’s **hemodynamic status after intervention**, including blood pressure, heart rate, and urine output.
- Any **transfusion requirements and the volume administered**.
- Whether the patient was **admitted for further observation or transferred to a higher-level facility**.
- The **final diagnosis or disposition**, such as “postpartum hemorrhage managed medically,” “hemorrhage with uterine atony,” or “hemorrhage requiring surgical intervention” [N4-F4].

The evidence also supports using standardized hemorrhage carts, ready access to uterotonics, and standardized stage-based management protocols to improve care [N5-F3]. It also emphasizes that standardized criteria should be available to distinguish PPH from normal postoperative or normal postpartum bleeding [N4-F4]. Therefore, the follow-up documentation should explicitly state whether the event met the PPH criteria and whether it was considered a complication.

## 5) When documentation should be completed during the event and after

Documentation should be completed as soon as the hemorrhage is recognized during the event and then completed in a timely manner afterward to preserve defensibility and continuity of care. The evidence from ACDIS notes that many drivers for coding PPH are related to processes and documentation rather than clinical causes, and that inconsistent documentation can make it hard to identify true hemorrhage cases [N4-F4]. It also states that accurate documentation of estimated blood loss is the cornerstone of identifying PPH early [N4-F4]. This means that documentation should not be delayed until after the event is resolved; rather, it should be captured promptly during the acute phase.

After the event, documentation should be completed promptly to preserve defensibility. ACDIS notes that coding pathways may default to PPH whenever uterine atony with a mention of bleeding is documented, even if the clinical picture does not meet the criteria [N4-F4]. Therefore, documentation after the event should be thorough enough to support the clinical judgment that the hemorrhage was excessive or a complication rather than routine postpartum bleeding. This includes documenting the provider’s assessment that the bleeding was not normal, the estimated blood loss, and the interventions taken [N4-F4].

## 6) Coding and billing implications

Coding and billing implications are heavily tied to documentation consistency. ACDIS states that coding pathways may lead to PPH being reported whenever uterine atony with bleeding is mentioned, even if the clinical picture does not meet the criteria [N4-F4]. It also notes that coding and CDI reviews should start with standardizing definitions, redesigning templates, improving documentation workflows, and expanding reviews into targeted cases [N4-F4]. This means that the documentation must be precise and aligned with ACOG’s definition of maternal hemorrhage.

The coding guidance also specifies that routine or expected hemorrhage during delivery should not be reported unless the provider documents that the bleeding is excessive or is a complication [N4-F4]. This implies that the documentation must clearly state whether the hemorrhage was abnormal and whether it met the criteria for PPH. If the documentation is unclear, coders should query the provider rather than report a code from ICD-10-CM category O72, Postpartum hemorrhage [N4-F4].

## 7) How to preserve defensibility and continuity of care

To preserve defensibility, documentation should be standardized, consistent, and defensible. ACDIS recommends standardizing definitions, redesigning templates, improving documentation workflows, and expanding reviews into targeted cases [N4-F4]. It also recommends that electronic templates be revised to include mandatory sections for estimated blood loss and that systems be programmed to convert measurements automatically to maintain consistency [N4-F4]. This supports the use of structured templates and prompts rather than relying on memory or inconsistent free text.

Continuity of care is preserved by documenting the hemorrhage in a way that can be understood by subsequent providers. The evidence emphasizes that documentation fulfills key functions including communication and quality assurance [N2-R3]. It also supports using standardized hemorrhage carts, ready access to uterotonics, and standardized stage-based management protocols to improve care [N5-F3]. Therefore, the documentation should include enough detail to allow others to understand the clinical course and the rationale for interventions.

## 8) Operational tools and templates to support documentation

The evidence base suggests that operational tools and templates should be adapted from standardized practice guidance, benchmarking systems, and electronic record design. ACOG recommends standardized bundles of care, including policies, guidelines, and algorithms, and notes that protocols and checklists can reduce patient harm through improved standardization and communication [N2-R2][N1-F1]. The ACDIS Q&A also stresses the importance of standardized definitions, redesigned templates, and electronic record improvements to address inconsistency in PPH documentation [N4-F4].

### Example documentation templates or scenarios
Although the evidence does not provide a single published ACOG template for postpartum hemorrhage, it does point to several relevant examples and scenarios:

- **ACOG obstetric patient record forms** can serve as a source for template design [N2-R1][N2-F2].
- **Stage-based hemorrhage protocols** are recommended to reduce delays in diagnosis and management [N5-F3].
- **In situ simulation scenarios** can be adapted into a training tool that reinforces the documentation elements needed during an actual hemorrhage event [N5-R4].
- **Risk assessment tools**, such as the AWHONN risk assessment tool, can be integrated into documentation templates as part of the hemorrhage risk assessment process [N5-R5].

### Checklists or protocols that can be adapted
The evidence strongly supports the use of checklists and protocols as practical tools for documentation and management:

- **Stage-based hemorrhage protocols** can be adapted into documentation templates that guide providers through recognition, intervention, and escalation [N5-F3].
- **Formal hemorrhage risk assessment at multiple points** in prenatal, delivery, and postpartum care can be turned into a checklist or protocol for documenting risk assessment throughout the care episode [N6-R4].
- **Estimated blood loss prompts** can be used as a checklist item to ensure consistent documentation [N4-F4].
- **Coding and CDI workflow checklists** can be adapted to improve defensibility and consistency [N4-F4].

### How to integrate documentation into clinical workflows
Documentation should be integrated into clinical workflows in ways that are efficient and do not distract from acute management. The evidence supports the following integration strategies:

- **Electronic prompts and alerts** for estimated blood loss, quantitative blood loss, and standardized documentation elements [N4-R4][N4-F4].
- **Standardized forms and templates**, including ACOG patient record forms and other standardized templates [N2-R1][N2-F2].
- **Training and simulation**, using in situ simulation scenarios to train providers on documentation and response during postpartum hemorrhage [N5-R4].
- **Multidisciplinary review and audit**, including standardizing definitions and expanding reviews into targeted cases [N4-F4].

## 9) Final recommended structure

Putting this together, the recommended structure for postpartum hemorrhage documentation should include:

1. **Event description**: time of onset, duration, bleeding characteristics, and whether it was recognized as abnormal.
2. **Blood loss measurement**: estimated or quantitative blood loss, method used, and any discrepancy [N4-F4][N5-F3].
3. **Clinical features**: signs and symptoms of hypovolemia, risk factors, and precipitating factors [N1-F1].
4. **Interventions and dosages**: sequence, type, route, and dose of interventions [N6-R3][N4-F4].
5. **Follow-up and disposition**: hemodynamic status, transfusion, admission, transfer, and final diagnosis [N4-F4].
6. **Alerts and prompts**: mandatory sections for estimated blood loss and standardized prompts to improve consistency [N4-F4].
7. **Coding and CDI defensibility**: clear statement that the bleeding was not normal and that it was clinically significant, with documentation aligned to ACOG’s PPH criteria [N4-F4][N1-F1].

## Bottom line

For an obstetrician, the best practice is to document postpartum hemorrhage in a structured, standardized, and defensible way that is tied to ACOG’s definition and management guidance. The documentation should be prompt during the event, complete afterward, and aligned with coding and billing standards. The evidence supports using templates, checklists, electronic prompts, and simulation-based training to make documentation efficient and consistent [N2-R2][N4-F4][N5-F3][N6-R4]. This approach strengthens both clinical care and defensibility.

- Whether the hemorrhage was recognized promptly and whether it was considered excessive or a complication [N4-F4].

- The sequence of interventions used, such as administration of uterotonics, manual removal of retained placenta, or uterine massage.
- Dosages and routes of administration for all drugs, including uterotonic agents and any transfusions [N4-F4].

- The patient’s hemodynamic status after intervention, including blood pressure, heart rate, and urine output.

1. **Event description**: Time, duration, bleeding characteristics, and whether it was recognized as abnormal.

The hemorrhage event should be documented with enough detail to support clinical decision-making and later review. Based on ACOG and related guidance, the documentation should include:

- **Time of onset and duration of bleeding**.
- **Estimated blood loss (EBL) or quantitative blood loss (QBL)**, including the method used and any discrepancy between provider estimate and measured value [N4-F4][N5-F3].
- **Clinical signs and symptoms of hypovolemia**, such as hypotension, tachycardia, pallor, or altered mental status [N1-F1].

ACOG guidance also supports standardized bundles of care and alerts, which help improve recognition and escalation [N1-F1][N6-R4]. ACOG recommends standardized bundles of care, including policies, guidelines, and algorithms, and notes that protocols and checklists can reduce patient harm through improved standardization and communication [N2-R2][N1-F1]. The ACDIS Q&A also stresses the importance of standardized definitions, redesigned templates, and electronic record improvements to address inconsistency in PPH documentation [N4-F4].

### Example documentation templates or scenarios
Although the evidence does not provide a single published ACOG template for postpartum hemorrhage, it does point to several relevant examples and scenarios:

- **ACOG obstetric patient record forms** can serve as a source for template design [N2-R1][N2-F2].
- **Stage-based hemorrhage protocols** are recommended to reduce delays in diagnosis and management [N5-F3].
- **In situ simulation scenarios** can be adapted into a training tool that reinforces the documentation elements needed during an actual hemorrhage event [N5-R4].
- **Risk assessment tools**, such as the AWHONN risk assessment tool, can be integrated into documentation templates as part of the hemorrhage risk assessment process [N5-R5].

### Checklists or protocols that can be adapted
The evidence strongly supports the use of checklists and protocols as practical tools for documentation and management:

- **Stage-based hemorrhage protocols** can be adapted into documentation templates that guide providers through recognition, intervention, and escalation [N5-F3].
- **Formal hemorrhage risk assessment at multiple points** in prenatal, delivery, and postpartum care can be turned into a checklist or protocol for documenting risk assessment throughout the care episode [N6-R4].

- **Coding and CDI workflow checklists** can be adapted to improve defensibility and consistency [N4-F4].

### How to integrate documentation into clinical workflows
Documentation should be integrated into clinical workflows in ways that are efficient and do not distract from acute management. The evidence supports the following integration strategies:

- **Electronic prompts and alerts** for estimated blood loss, quantitative blood loss, and standardized documentation elements [N4-R4][N4-F4].
- **Standardized forms and templates**, including ACOG patient record forms and other standardized templates [N2-R1][N2-F2].
- **Training and simulation**, using in situ simulation scenarios to train providers on documentation and response during postpartum hemorrhage [N5-R4].
- **Multidisciplinary review and audit**, including standardizing definitions and expanding reviews into targeted cases [N4-F4].

## 9) Final recommended structure

Putting this together, the recommended structure for postpartum hemorrhage documentation should include:

1. **Event description**: time of onset, duration, bleeding characteristics, and whether it was recognized as abnormal.
2. **Blood loss measurement**: estimated or quantitative blood loss, method used, and any discrepancy [N4-F4][N5-F3].
3. **Clinical features**: signs and symptoms of hypovolemia, risk factors, and precipitating factors [N1-F1].
4. **Interventions and dosages**: sequence, type, route, and dose of interventions [N6-R3][N4-F4].
5. **Follow-up and disposition**: hemodynamic status, transfusion, admission, transfer, and final diagnosis [N4-F4].
6. **Alerts and prompts**: mandatory sections for estimated blood loss and standardized prompts to improve consistency [N4-F4].
7. **Coding and CDI defensibility**: clear statement that the bleeding was not normal and that it was clinically significant, with documentation aligned to ACOG’s PPH criteria [N4-F4][N1-F1].

## Bottom line

For an obstetrician, the best practice is to document postpartum hemorrhage in a structured, standardized, and defensible way that is tied to ACOG’s definition and management guidance. The documentation should be prompt during the event, complete afterward, and aligned with coding and billing standards. The evidence supports using templates, checklists, electronic prompts, and simulation-based training to make documentation efficient and consistent [N2-R2][N4-F4][N5-F3][N6-R4]. This approach strengthens both clinical care and defensibility.
